# Reconstructing the Internet Research Agency’s 2016 Social-Media Influence Operation

## Executive assessment

The evidence supports a concrete conclusion: the Internet Research Agency (IRA) conducted a Russian-funded, industrial-scale influence operation that used fabricated American identities, coordinated social-media accounts, paid advertising, stolen personal information, U.S.-based technical infrastructure, and offline political events to influence and polarize American audiences. The operation was not limited to conventional pro-Donald Trump messaging. Its broader objective was to exploit existing racial, ideological, religious, and political divisions, undermine confidence in democratic institutions, damage Hillary Clinton’s candidacy, and support Donald Trump where possible.

The Department of Justice indictment describes the conduct as an alleged criminal conspiracy involving the IRA, Yevgeniy Prigozhin, Concord-related companies, and numerous IRA employees. The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence subsequently assessed—based on company-provided platform data, law-enforcement material, and expert analysis—that the Russian government tasked and supported the IRA’s interference campaign. The evidence therefore links five components: organizational control, financial sponsorship, operational methods, audience targeting, and electoral objectives. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Source and evidentiary framework

Four provided sources are used in this report:

- **S1:** U.S. Department of Justice indictment in *United States v. Internet Research Agency et al.*, filed February 16, 2018. This source contains allegations made in a federal indictment and should not be treated as a final adjudication of every factual allegation.
- **S2:** NPR’s October 8, 2019 summary of the Senate Intelligence Committee’s findings. This is a secondary report and is used mainly to clarify the public significance of the Senate findings.
- **S3:** Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, *Russian Active Measures Campaigns and Interference in the 2016 U.S. Election, Volume 2: Russia’s Use of Social Media*. This is the principal source for platform data, committee findings, and expert analysis.
- **S4:** Philip Howard and colleagues’ report, *The IRA, Social Media and Political Polarization in the United States, 2012–2018*, released through the University of Nebraska–Lincoln Digital Commons. This report summarizes analysis of social-media data supplied to the Senate Committee. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S2](https://www.npr.org/2019/10/08/768319934/senate-report-russians-used-used-social-media-mostly-to-target-race-in-2016); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf); [S4](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/senatedocs/1/))

## Organizational structure and funding

### The IRA and Project Lakhta

The indictment identifies the IRA as a Russian organization headquartered in St. Petersburg and operating from an office at 55 Savushkina Street. It states that the organization used several associated or substitute entities, including Internet Research LLC, MediaSintez LLC, GlavSet LLC, MixInfo LLC, Azimut LLC, and NovInfo LLC. The IRA reportedly employed hundreds of workers across graphics, data analysis, search-engine optimization, information technology, finance, and social-media operations. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The U.S. indictment describes the American-facing “translator project,” established by approximately April 2014. By July 2016, more than 80 employees were assigned to it. The project focused on YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter and was allegedly directed to create political intensity by supporting radical groups, dissatisfied users, and oppositional movements. The stated election-related objective was to “spread distrust towards the candidates and the political system in general.” ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The Senate report connects the IRA to Yevgeniy Prigozhin and describes him as the organization’s funder and director. The indictment more specifically alleges that Prigozhin controlled Concord Management and Consulting and Concord Catering, which funded and supervised the IRA’s interference activities. The indictment calls this larger operation “Project Lakhta.” By September 2016, the monthly Project Lakhta budget reportedly exceeded 73 million Russian rubles, described in the indictment as more than $1.25 million, including approximately one million rubles in bonuses. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

The alleged funding architecture was deliberately indirect. The indictment states that Concord labeled payments as software support and development and routed money through approximately fourteen affiliated Russian entities. This indicates an effort to conceal the relationship between the funding source and the influence operation. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

### Key personnel

The indictment identifies a management hierarchy. Mikhail Bystrov allegedly served as general director and highest-ranking employee; Mikhail Burchik allegedly served as executive director and managed operational planning, infrastructure, and personnel. Aleksandra Krylova and Anna Bogacheva allegedly participated in a 2014 U.S. reconnaissance trip. Sergey Polozov allegedly managed the IT department and procured U.S.-based servers and infrastructure. Dzheyhun Aslanov allegedly headed the translator project during the 2016 election period, while Gleb Vasilchenko, Irina Kaverzina, Vladimir Venkov, and others allegedly operated false American personas and posted content. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

These roles indicate a division of labor resembling a communications organization rather than a loose collection of independent internet users. Research, persona development, content production, account management, advertising, financial processing, infrastructure concealment, and performance measurement were handled as distinct operational functions. This assessment is consistent with the Senate report’s description of a professionalized “troll factory” using large numbers of employees and multiple specialized teams. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Operational methods

### Reconnaissance and audience research

The indictment alleges that Krylova and Bogacheva traveled through several U.S. states in June 2014 under false pretenses. Their itinerary included Nevada, California, New Mexico, Colorado, Illinois, Michigan, Louisiana, Texas, and New York. They allegedly carried cameras, SIM cards, and “drop phones,” and discussed security and evacuation procedures. Their purpose, according to the indictment, was to collect intelligence for the IRA’s future U.S. operations. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The operation also monitored U.S. social-media groups, tracking group size, posting frequency, and engagement levels. IRA personnel allegedly studied American political and social communities to identify issues, audiences, and geographic locations that could be mobilized. In one example, a false persona communicated with a Texas-based grassroots activist and was advised to focus on “purple states like Colorado, Virginia & Florida.” ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

### Fabricated American identities

The IRA created hundreds of accounts designed to appear to be operated by Americans. Specialists allegedly worked day and night shifts aligned with U.S. time zones and used U.S. holidays and culturally familiar subjects to make the accounts appear authentic. Their content covered U.S. foreign policy, economic issues, immigration, religion, race, policing, firearms, and regional identity. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The Senate’s analysis characterizes this as a credibility-building process. Accounts often began with ordinary or apparently nonpolitical content, cultivated followers, and only later introduced “payload” messages designed to provoke or influence audiences. For example, the “Army of Jesus” Facebook page primarily posted religious material before publishing an anti-Clinton message shortly before the election. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

### Concealed infrastructure and stolen identities

The indictment alleges that IRA personnel purchased U.S.-based server space and created virtual private networks. Russian operators could then connect through U.S. infrastructure, masking their Russian origin when opening accounts, communicating with Americans, and managing social-media pages. They also allegedly created hundreds of email accounts under false names. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The operation allegedly used Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, fake driver’s licenses, bank accounts, credit cards, and PayPal accounts belonging to real Americans or fictitious personas. The indictment identifies alleged use of stolen identities to open U.S. financial accounts, evade PayPal security controls, buy advertising, fund rallies, and pay for promotional posts. These allegations formed the basis for wire-fraud, bank-fraud, and aggravated-identity-theft counts. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

## Campaign objectives and narratives

### Anti-Clinton and pro-Trump activity

The indictment alleges that by 2016 the IRA’s operations primarily sought to denigrate Hillary Clinton, criticize other candidates such as Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio, support Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump, and increase distrust in the political system. Internal instructions reportedly told specialists to criticize Clinton and other candidates while exempting Sanders and Trump from criticism. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The Senate Committee assessed that the IRA sought to harm Clinton and support Trump at the direction of the Kremlin. Its analysis found that Clinton was the only major presidential candidate whose IRA references were uniformly negative, while Trump received predominantly positive treatment before the election. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

The evidence does not support reducing the entire operation to a simple pro-Trump advertising campaign. Most content did not explicitly name either presidential candidate. Instead, it promoted narratives of social conflict, hopelessness, distrust, and contempt for political opponents. The Senate Committee specifically concluded that the election was part of a broader campaign to exploit societal divisions. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

### Racial targeting and voter suppression

African-American audiences were the most heavily targeted group identified by the Senate Committee. More than 66 percent of IRA Facebook advertisements reportedly contained a race-related term. The “Blacktivist” page generated approximately 11.2 million engagements, five of the ten most-followed IRA Instagram accounts focused on African-American issues, and approximately 96 percent of IRA YouTube videos concerned race or police brutality. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf); [S2](https://www.npr.org/2019/10/08/768319934/senate-report-russians-used-used-social-media-mostly-to-target-race-in-2016))

The campaign used different messages for different audiences. Conservative audiences were encouraged to support Trump, while African-American and other likely Clinton voters were targeted with messages urging them not to vote, to distrust the electoral system, or to support third-party candidate Jill Stein. The Senate report describes this asymmetry as evidence of voter-suppression objectives rather than merely ideological persuasion. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

### Inciting opposing groups

A particularly important tactic was the simultaneous activation of opposing sides. The IRA reportedly used “Heart of Texas” to promote an anti-Islam event in Houston while using “United Muslims of America” to promote a counter-event at the same location and time. The Senate report states that the objective was to produce confrontation between groups that did not know they were being manipulated by the same foreign operation. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

This pattern demonstrates the operation’s broader strategic logic: ideological consistency was less important than polarization. The IRA could support mutually incompatible positions if both generated anger, distrust, and social conflict. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Platform footprint and reach

| Platform | Documented activity | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---:|---|
| Facebook | Approximately 61,500 organic posts, 3,393 paid advertisements, 81 analyzed pages; as many as 126 million U.S. users may have encountered IRA content | Major audience-building and event-coordination platform |
| Instagram | Approximately 116,000 posts across 133 accounts; about 187 million engagements reported in the Senate analysis | Particularly effective for racial, cultural, and identity-based messaging |
| Twitter | Approximately 10.4 million tweets across 3,841 accounts in the Senate dataset; more than 3,800 IRA-linked accounts identified | High-volume amplification, persona interaction, and hashtag manipulation |
| YouTube | Approximately 1,100 videos totaling 43 hours across 17 channels | Primarily used for race and police-brutality content |
| Reddit and Tumblr | Approximately 944 suspicious Reddit accounts and 84 IRA-linked Tumblr accounts identified | Testing narratives, reaching niche communities, and cultivating young audiences |

([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf); [S4](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/senatedocs/1/))

The Senate report emphasizes that paid advertising was only a small part of the operation. Facebook estimated approximately $100,000 in IRA advertising over two years, while the IRA’s broader operational budget was estimated at approximately $1.25 million per month. The larger impact came from organic posts, fake personas, shares, reposts, and engagement by unwitting Americans. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Offline political activity

The IRA extended online influence into physical events. The indictment alleges that false personas organized “March for Trump,” “Down with Hillary,” “Florida Goes Trump,” “Miners for Trump,” and other rallies. Operators allegedly purchased advertising, contacted grassroots groups, communicated with Trump campaign personnel, recruited volunteers, paid participants, and arranged for a person to portray Clinton in a prison costume beside a cage built on a flatbed truck. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf))

The Senate report identifies at least 130 Facebook events promoted through IRA-linked pages. Approximately 338,300 genuine accounts engaged with event-related content, 62,500 users indicated an intention to attend, and another 25,800 expressed interest. These figures measure platform interactions and declared interest, not verified attendance. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Timeline

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| 2013 | IRA registered as a Russian corporate entity; U.S.-focused Twitter activity began by approximately this period |
| 2014 | Translator project established; Krylova and Bogacheva conducted U.S. reconnaissance; election interference planning allegedly began |
| 2015 | Facebook and Instagram operations expanded; IRA experimented with rallies and offline mobilization |
| Early 2016 | Internal instructions emphasized anti-Clinton and pro-Trump messaging |
| June–September 2016 | False personas organized rallies and communicated with U.S. activists and Trump campaign contacts |
| October–November 2016 | Voter-fraud narratives, anti-voting messages, anti-Clinton advertisements, and pro-Trump activity intensified |
| After Election Day | IRA activity increased rather than stopped, shifting toward post-election conflict, anti-Trump and pro-Trump mobilization, and broader social issues |
| September 2017 | Facebook disclosed Russian-linked advertising; IRA personnel allegedly began destroying evidence |
| February 2018 | DOJ indictment publicly described the alleged criminal conspiracy |

([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf); [S4](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/senatedocs/1/))

## Contradictions and unresolved issues

The sources contain several important evidentiary qualifications.

First, the Senate report states that Facebook-linked IRA advertisements generally did not use the most sophisticated “Custom Audiences” tool. Senator Wyden’s additional views, however, state that Facebook acknowledged IRA use of custom audiences based on engagement with particular IRA pages. These accounts may concern different forms of custom-audience functionality, but the provided sources do not fully resolve the discrepancy. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

Second, the Senate report presents different estimates for Instagram reach: Facebook representatives reportedly estimated that Instagram content reached approximately 20 million users, while the independent analysis emphasized much larger engagement figures and suggested that the platform estimate might be incomplete. Reach and engagement are different measurements, but the sources acknowledge unresolved methodological uncertainty. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

Third, the indictment alleges criminal conduct but does not itself establish convictions. The Senate Committee’s attribution of Kremlin direction is an investigative finding, not a criminal verdict against every named person or an independently litigated finding in the indictment. This distinction matters when describing the evidence. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/d9/fieldable-panel-panes/basic-panes/attachments/2018/02/16/internet_research_agency_indictment.pdf); [S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf))

## Conclusion

The most defensible reconstruction is that the IRA operated as a centrally funded and professionally organized influence enterprise. It built apparently American online identities, studied U.S. audiences, concealed Russian infrastructure, exploited stolen identities and financial accounts, disseminated high-volume content across multiple platforms, targeted racial and ideological fault lines, encouraged selective voter suppression, supported Trump and opposed Clinton before the election, and staged or promoted real-world events.

The operation’s defining feature was not simply propaganda in favor of one candidate. It was the systematic manufacture of apparently domestic political activity by a foreign organization. The IRA’s central strategic advantage came from combining audience cultivation with timed, divisive “payload” content and from making real Americans unknowingly extend the operation’s reach. The Senate evidence also indicates that the campaign continued and expanded after Election Day, supporting the conclusion that its broader objective was to weaken trust and intensify political conflict rather than merely influence a single vote. ([S3](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume2.pdf); [S4](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/senatedocs/1/))
